channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Why intimate partner violence can be a barrier to breastfeeding
item.description: When a mother struggles to breastfeed, it is not always obvious why. But a meta-analysis from a University of Wollongong (UOW) Ph.D. candidate has revealed that intimate partner violence (IPV) in the perinatal period could play a hidden role.

item.title: New research identifies potentially overlooked factor in male fertility
item.description: A new study conducted by a team of researchers at the Wayne State University School of Medicine suggests that men can show normal semen analysis results yet harbor a sperm characteristic associated with a reduced likelihood of achieving pregnancy with their partners.

item.title: Food delivery apps: An emerging public health challenge
item.description: Food delivery giants including Uber Eats and DoorDash may be fueling Australia's growing obesity crisis, with new research showing their platforms are bombarding consumers with junk food promotions and encouraging poor eating habits.

item.title: Nerve signaling pathway reveals how a tuberculosis molecule triggers cough
item.description: A molecule produced by some highly transmissible strains of tuberculosis (TB) bacteria activates sensory nerves and triggers coughing, according to a study led by UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers. The findings, published in Nature Microbiology, uncover a signaling pathway that could be targeted with drugs developed for chronic cough, offering a possible approach to relieving TB-associated cough and reducing transmission.

item.title: Molecular backdoor destroys 'undruggable' protein driving rare childhood cancer
item.description: A secret molecular backdoor let researchers from Penn State College of Medicine destroy a protein that drives a rare and often fatal bone and soft tissue cancer in children and adolescents that often returns in treatment-resistant forms. Now, just three years after the discovery, a Phase I clinical trial is underway and, once complete, a Phase II trial to test the approach's efficacy in patients will follow shortly thereafter.

item.title: Q&A: Can short, animated videos boost screen mindfulness?
item.description: Smartphones are an indispensable part of daily life, but many young adults struggle with compulsive scrolling, late-night use and feeling anxious whenever their phones aren't nearby. Researchers at Stanford Medicine worked with young adults at Avenues the World School in New York City to co-design short, animated videos aimed at boosting awareness of the risks of overusing our phones.

item.title: How brain aging differs from neurodegeneration: New data could help in the search for dementia drugs
item.description: Researchers from Skoltech, together with colleagues from Ben-Gurion University (Israel) and other organizations, studied how the spatial organization of DNA in neurons changes during natural aging and in the development of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's. The results showed that, although chromatin regulation is disrupted during aging, the onset of neurodegenerative diseases is driven by an additional factor—the accumulation of DNA damage.

item.title: Study confirms link between autism and GI symptoms in children
item.description: Researchers at UTHealth Houston have confirmed that children with autism spectrum disorder who experience greater challenges with social awareness and communication may also be more likely to have severe gastrointestinal symptoms.

item.title: Salt reduction could maximize kidney drug benefits
item.description: Reducing salt intake to guideline-recommended levels could substantially enhance the kidney-protective effects of an emerging class of treatments for chronic kidney disease, a study suggests.

item.title: How the intestine keeps its tremendous surface area in order
item.description: The small intestine is constantly in flux. This 20-foot-long (6.1-meter-long) tube is lined with structures that absorb the nutrients during digestion. The cells at the tip of these structures are continuously replaced, but how they stay organized has not been well understood.

item.title: Dual inhibition of transcriptional kinases and anti-apoptotic proteins targets tumor growth
item.description: In cancer research, the protein kinases CDK12 and CDK13 are attracting attention as promising targets for therapy. These enzymes regulate gene transcription by phosphorylating—transferring a phosphate group to—the protein complex RNA polymerase II, which transcribes DNA. Inhibiting CDK12 and CDK13 disrupts the transcription of particularly long genes, which leads to defects in DNA damage repair and thus the suppression of cancer cell proliferation.

item.title: Mental health chatbots for kids? Parents narrow eyes
item.description: Despite a shortage of therapists and a mental health crisis affecting the nation's youth, parents aren't ready to call on AI chatbots as therapeutic reinforcements, according to a new study from Harvard and Boston Children's Hospital.

item.title: Flu shots linked to lower mortality reach few unvaccinated heart attack patients in Swedish hospitals
item.description: Influenza vaccination after a heart attack can reduce the risk of death during the following year. This has been shown in previous research from Sweden and international collaborations.

item.title: What role do immune cells in the lens play in uveitis?
item.description: Uveitis, an autoimmune disease that causes inflammation in the eye, can cause blindness if not adequately treated. There is often no identifiable cause of uveitis, making it difficult to intervene before the disease progresses, but identifying the early changes in the disease could improve detection.

item.title: Court-appointed medical guardian study reveals role in care of highly vulnerable older adults
item.description: When University of Michigan Health geriatrician Kahli Zietlow, M.D., gets summoned to the hospital room of a seriously ill older adult, she knows the assessments she performs might help determine if the patient can make their own medical decisions or if someone else will have to. But if the patient's health or mental capacity has declined too far before they could legally authorize someone to make medical decisions for them, then Zietlow knows that the hospital may ask a probate court to assign a guardian to make those decisions, either temporarily or permanently.

item.title: AI-powered lifestyle modification chatbot offers advice, accountability, affordability
item.description: Many of the 79% of American adults trying to improve their diet and exercise habits seek guidance. But personal coaches are expensive, and self-help lifestyle apps, while affordable, lack accountability.

item.title: Lung complications affect 1 in 3 patients receiving antibody-drug conjugates for lung cancer, study finds
item.description: A study led by The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center—Arthur G. James Cancer Hospital and Richard J. Solove Research Institute (OSUCCC—James) sheds light on safety concerns as antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) become more important in lung cancer treatment. The findings highlight the need to catch and manage side effects like lung toxicity much earlier to help patients safely benefit from ADCs.

item.title: Single vaping episode impairs vascular function, study finds
item.description: Researchers have identified acute negative effects of vaping, even without nicotine, on vascular function. The results of the study are being presented next week at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA).

item.title: Elevated blood sugar levels over decades linked to worse midlife memory and cognitive function
item.description: Young adults with a progressive rise in fasting blood sugar levels over multiple decades were more likely to have worse cognitive health by midlife. Participants who developed type 2 diabetes during the study also had signs of structural brain changes, according to new, independent research published in the Journal of the American Heart Association.

item.title: Early-stage breast cancer gains first newly approved hormone therapy in more than 20 years
item.description: For the first time in more than two decades, the FDA has approved a new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer, marking a monumental shift in how the most common form of the disease is treated.

item.title: A doctor's take on the US losing measles elimination status
item.description: For many physicians of my generation, measles was a disease we rarely—or never—saw in practice. That was a sign of how well vaccination and public health efforts had worked.

item.title: Drones could soon fly blood, defibrillators and medicine to patients
item.description: Paramedics in one Florida county may soon be able to call in a drone to bring blood to a patient who's bleeding heavily.

item.title: Disrupting a developing brain circuit in adolescence may have lasting social effects
item.description: Adolescence is often described as a turbulent period of life marked by growing independence, changing social relationships and unpredictable shifts in behavior. According to researchers, tweens' and teens' behavioral changes reflect a brain that is still actively developing, yet scientists know surprisingly little about the neural mechanisms that shape social behavior during this critical stage of life.

item.title: England shows widest socioeconomic gap in frailty among 31 countries
item.description: Older adults from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds experience greater levels of frailty, with England showing the biggest gap between socioeconomic groups among the 31 countries studied.

item.title: Prior authorization limits help expand opioid addiction treatment where approvals were a frequent roadblock, study finds
item.description: State laws limiting prior authorization requirements for opioid use disorder medications were associated with increased buprenorphine use in Medicaid, but only in states where those requirements were frequent barriers to access, according to a new study led by University of Michigan researchers.

item.title: FDA approves bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib as new second-line therapy for patients with GIST
item.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a combination of bezuclastinib plus sunitinib as second-line therapy after first-line treatment with imatinib for adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) based on evidence from the phase 3 PEAK study led by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute showing that the combination outperformed standard therapy with sunitinib alone.

item.title: Reducing or quitting smoking linked to lower risk for developing psoriasis
item.description: Smoking reduction is associated with a reduced risk for developing psoriasis, including psoriasis vulgaris (PsV) and palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), according to a research letter published online Nov. 18 in JAMA Dermatology.

item.title: Inflammatory bowel disease linked to increased risk for cirrhosis
item.description: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), especially ulcerative colitis, is associated with an increased risk for cirrhosis diagnosis, according to a study recently published in Sage Open Chronic Diseases.

item.title: FDA approves Nelkarmi for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer
item.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has granted approval to Nelkarmi (neladalkib), a kinase inhibitor, for adults with locally advanced or metastatic anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who were previously treated. The approval was granted to Nuvalent and GSK.

item.title: Common patterns of b/tsDMARD use identified in rheumatoid arthritis
item.description: Common patterns of biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (b/tsDMARD) use are seen among patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and these patterns are associated with underlying genetic associations, according to a study published online Nov. 20 in Arthritis & Rheumatology.
